questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: group the words of one everyday domain into a usable family
questions.stem: A tenant reads 'Die Miete ist gestiegen, deshalb muss ich zum Monatsende kündigen.' Which six words make up one vocabulary family here?

options.text: Miete, kündigen, Vermieter, Nebenkosten, Kaution and umziehen
Miete, kündigen, Fahrplan, Umstieg, Verspätung and Kofferraum
options.misconception: mixes the housing family with the travel family

options.text: Besprechung, Antrag, Frist, Protokoll, Unterschrift and Akte
options.misconception: mixes the housing family with the office family

options.text: Miete, kündigen, Zinsen, Aktie, Anleihe and Börse
options.misconception: mixes the housing family with the finance family

questions.explanation: A vocabulary family is a set of words that travel through one area of life and support each other, so Miete, Vermieter, Nebenkosten, Kaution, kündigen and umziehen belong together in a story about a flat. The test is whether the words can be used in the same set of sentences about the same topic, and housing words pass it because every one of them has something to do with a tenancy. The value of learning in families is that one unknown word is easier to place when its neighbours are known, and it is also easier to remember, since the family supplies the context in which the new word will turn up.
questions.hint: Ask which set of words could all appear in a letter about one tenant's flat.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: group the words of one everyday domain into a usable family
questions.stem: A notice at a station reads 'Der Zug hat zwei Minuten Verspätung. Der Umstieg erfolgt in Halle drei.' Which six words belong to the same family?

options.text: Verspätung, Umstieg, Fahrplan, Abfahrt, Gleis and Anschluss
Verspätung, Umstieg, Miete, Nebenkosten, Kaution and Vermieter
options.misconception: mixes the travel family with the housing family

options.text: Fahrplan, Abfahrt, Gleis, Antrag, Frist and Unterschrift
options.misconception: mixes the travel family with the office family

options.text: Anschluss, Gleis, Abfahrt, Kaffee, Semmel and Sahne
options.misconception: mixes the travel family with the breakfast family

questions.explanation: The travel family is built from the nouns a passenger meets in a station: der Fahrplan, die Abfahrt, das Gleis, die Verspätung, der Umstieg for changing trains, and der Anschluss for a connecting service. Two of them, umsteigen and der Umstieg, are a noun and a verb from the same root, and that kind of pairing is common in German and worth exploiting when building a family. A learner who knows the family can guess the sense of an unfamiliar member from the company it keeps, which is a far firmer clue than any dictionary gloss in a language where compounds are so frequent.
questions.hint: Ask which words would all appear on the same station sign or ticket.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: group the words of one everyday domain into a usable family
questions.stem: A starter pack for a new clerk contains six words. Which set belongs together as one family?

options.text: Antrag, einreichen, Frist, Besprechung, Protokoll and Unterschrift
Antrag, einreichen, Frist, Verspätung, Umstieg and Gleis
options.misconception: mixes the office family with the travel family

options.text: Antrag, einreichen, Frist, Miete, Kaution and Nebenkosten
options.misconception: mixes the office family with the housing family

options.text: Antrag, einreichen, Frist, Semmel, Sahne und Rotkraut
options.misconception: mixes the office family with the regional food family

questions.explanation: An office family gathers around the paperwork a clerk handles every day: der Antrag is the application, einreichen is to hand it in, die Frist is the deadline, die Besprechung is the meeting, das Protokoll is the record of it and die Unterschrift is the signature that closes the file. Two further members fit the same set of sentences, namely der Vorgang for the file and die Abteilung for the department, and adding them costs nothing. The point of the family is predictive rather than decorative: a learner who can place an unknown word beside Frist and Protokoll has a real chance of understanding it in an article about administrative work.
questions.hint: Ask which words would appear in the same job description.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: recognise a German word whose English look-alike means something else
questions.stem: On a shelf label a learner reads 'Vorsicht, das Gift' and translates it as danger, gift. What does the German word actually denote?

options.text: Poison, so a correct rendering is a warning about something toxic
A present left behind, so the label asks visitors not to take it
options.misconception: reads an English look-alike and misses that the sense has moved

options.text: A debt owed to the shop, which has to be paid before leaving
options.misconception: invents a financial sense for a word that has none here

options.text: A favour owed to a colleague, which the label asks the reader to return
options.misconception: extends an English sense into a German word that does not use it

questions.explanation: Das Gift means poison, and the usual warning on a shelf is precisely that: something here is toxic, not something here was left as a present. It is a false friend in the strict sense, because the word looks exactly like the English gift while belonging to a different family of meanings, and the plural die Gifte and the adjective giftig confirm the field. A small number of these pairs exist in every language, and they are the most dangerous vocabulary to meet late, because the error is invisible in writing and only surfaces when the learner uses the word and is misunderstood.
questions.hint: Ask what a chemist would call the contents of the bottle.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: separate German Rente from the English word rent
questions.stem: A leaflet says 'Die Rente wird im Alter ausgezahlt.' Why would a learner who reads rent in English get this sentence wrong?

options.text: Rente is a pension paid later in life, while rent as a payment is die Miete
Rente is a payment for a flat, so the sentence is really about a tenancy
options.misconception: uses the English sense and misses that the two words are distinct

options.text: Rente is a tax on wages, so the sentence concerns an employer's costs
options.misconception: confuses a pension with a payroll deduction

options.text: Rente is a fee for a course, so the sentence is about adult education
options.misconception: assigns a fee sense the German word does not carry

questions.explanation: Die Rente is what a pension system pays after retirement, so the sentence is about an income later in life, and the same word covers company pensions in die betriebliche Rente. The English rent, the monthly charge for a flat, is die Miete in German, and a learner who imports the English sense produces a sentence about housing where the text is about retirement. The distinction is reinforced by the neighbours of the word, since Rentenversicherung and Rentenversicherte are unmistakably about pensions, and by the absence of die Rente in a rental contract, which always says Miete.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two words a landlord's contract would use.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: keep German Ertrag apart from the English verb it resembles
questions.stem: A business report says 'Der Ertrag des Betriebes ist gesunken.' A learner reads the word as engage. What does it mean here?

options.text: The yield or revenue earned by the business, which has gone down
A promise of employment, which the business has withdrawn
options.misconception: reads an English look-alike and takes the sense of a job contract

options.text: The building the business works in, which has been sold
options.misconception: confuses income with the premises a firm occupies

options.text: The effort needed to produce goods, which has grown
options.misconception: turns a revenue figure into an input measure

questions.explanation: Der Ertrag is what something yields: the revenue of a business, the yield of a field, the income from a property. In a report the figure is money coming in, so gesunken says it has fallen, and the neighbours of the word, der Ertrag eines Werks and die Erträge eines Feldes, keep the sense of an output in view. The cognate trap is the verb ertragen, which means to bear or endure, as in Diese Last kann ich nicht ertragen, so a learner who meets ertragen in a novel and reads it as to earn will also misread the noun it belongs to.
questions.hint: Ask whether the figure is money coming in or a promise made to a worker.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: recognise a cognate whose German sense has moved away
questions.stem: A learner sees die Uhr on a train ticket platform and reaches for English hour. What has happened to this word over time?

options.text: It still means an hour, and a clock as well, so the ticket office sells none of them
It drifted from the measure of time to the object that measures it
options.misconception: believes the German word covers only a stretch of time

options.text: It drifted from a piece of time to the person who counts the hours for a wage
options.misconception: turns a cognate into a claim about a worker

options.text: It drifted from a clock to a public holiday that falls on a Sunday
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the change and invents a festival

questions.explanation: Die Uhr covers both an hour and a clock, and a station sign uses it in the second sense while a timetable uses die Stunde or das Verzeichnis der Abfahrtszeiten. The cognate is genuine, since German Uhr and English hour come from the same root and once meant the same thing, so the pair is a good example of a word whose range of meanings has widened rather than shifted. A drifted cognate is harder to spot than a false friend, because part of the meaning still overlaps, and that partial overlap is exactly what makes the remaining part slip through unnoticed.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two English senses a sign pointing at a platform would use.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: handle a cognate that carries an extra German sense
questions.stem: A translator has to render das Schloss in a brochure about a hilltop building and reaches for English lock. What is wrong with that choice?

options.text: Das Schloss means a castle and a lock, and only the second sense matches English lock
Das Schloss means only a lock, so a brochure about a building needs das Schloss nicht
options.misconception: assumes the cognate kept a single sense in both languages

options.text: Das Schloss is a drill for walls, so a building text should say die Bohrung
options.misconception: invents a tool sense the German word does not have

options.text: Das Schloss is a hinge, so the correct word for a lock is das Gelenk
options.misconception: confuses a fastening device with a joint

questions.explanation: Das Schloss is a single German word with two senses, the lock on a door and the castle of a king, and the second is the older of the two. English split the pair: the lock kept the word, while the castle became an unrelated word, so the two languages now package the same idea differently. This is the reverse of a false friend, since the cognate relationship is real and one side has simply added a meaning. A translator who reaches for lock in a text about a hilltop building produces a sentence that is comprehensible in a photograph and wrong in the text.
questions.hint: Ask which sense a word for a fortified building would require.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: handle a cognate whose German sense is unrelated to the English one
questions.stem: A learner writes 'Sie zahlt eine Fee für die Reparatur' and a speaker looks puzzled. What went wrong with the word?

options.text: Die Fee is a fairy, so the sentence should use die Gebühr for a charge
Die Fee is a small animal, so the sentence describes a pet and not a payment
options.misconception: invents a third sense that belongs to neither language

options.text: Die Fee is a relative, so the sentence names a family member instead of a sum
options.misconception: treats the cognate as if it kept the English sense

options.text: Die Fee is a fee, but it must stand after the noun it qualifies in German
options.misconception: accepts the false sense and invents a word-order rule to defend it

questions.explanation: Die Fee is a fairy, in a fairy tale, and the German word for a charge is die Gebühr, as in eine Gebühr von zwölf Euro. The pair is a clean case of a cognate whose senses have nothing to do with each other in the two languages, which is more useful for a learner than a merely partial overlap because the mistake is obvious once it is seen. Two further members of the same family, die_fee? no: die Elfe, the elf, and der Zwerg, the dwarf, show that the vocabulary of the fairy tale is intact and worth learning as a set.
questions.hint: Ask who appears at the end of a story in a wood and is called die Fee.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: describe what a separable prefix adds to the base verb
questions.stem: A learner notices anrufen, ausgeben and einladen and asks what the three prefixes have in common. Which answer fits?

options.text: Each adds a direction or a limit to a plain verb, so a phone call gets a recipient
Each turns a verb into a noun, so a call and an invitation become things
options.misconception: believes every prefix turns the verb into a countable noun

options.text: Each marks the past, so all three verbs behave like strong verbs
options.misconception: confuses a prefix with a marker of tense

options.text: Each makes the verb transitive, so an object becomes grammatically necessary
options.misconception: believes a prefix settles whether an object is required

questions.explanation: A separable prefix usually narrows a plain verb by adding direction, contact or completion. Rufen is simply to call or shout, anrufen is to call someone on the phone, ausgeben is to hand out or pay out, and laden is to load or invite while einladen is to invite someone in. The effect on meaning is consistent enough to be worth stating as a rule of thumb, which is a rare piece of regularity for German vocabulary, and it gives a learner a way to guess the sense of an unfamiliar prefixed verb from the sense of its base.
questions.hint: Ask what rufen, geben and laden mean before the prefix is attached.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: describe how a prefix changes the limits of a verb
questions.stem: A learner pairs stehen with aufstehen and hören with aufhören. What does the prefix contribute in each new verb?

options.text: It marks the start and the end of the plain action rather than adding a new object
It marks the start and the end of the plain action and always adds an object
options.misconception: believes a prefixed verb always needs an object

options.text: It changes the tense, so the new verbs belong to the past of the plain ones
options.misconception: reads the prefix as a marker of past time

options.text: It makes the verbs reflexive, so the subject acts on itself
options.misconception: believes auf forces a reflexive pronoun

questions.explanation: Prefixes of this family describe the shape of an action rather than its participants: aufstehen is the opposite of sich hinlegen, and aufhören is the opposite of anfangen, so both tell the listener where an activity stands. A third member of the same family is ankommen, which reports the completion of a journey and is one of the reasons the auxiliary sein comes up so often. None of these verbs needs an object, and the prefix has no effect on tense, which is why a learner who expects the prefix to supply a subject runs out of words after the finite part.
questions.hint: Ask what aufstehen and aufhören have in common with anfangen and ankommen.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: read the extra sense a prefix adds to a base verb
questions.stem: A notice says 'Anfang zwölf hört die Schule auf, und die Kinder kommen mit.' What do the two prefixed verbs contribute?

options.text: Anfangen marks a beginning and mitkommen adds the company of the children
Anfangen marks an ending and mitkommen removes the children from the group
options.misconception: believes mit always subtracts the second participant

options.text: Both prefixes mark a time, so the sentence is a report about the clock only
options.misconception: reduces both prefixes to temporal reference

options.text: Both prefixes are inseparable, so they stay attached to the finite verb
options.misconception: misclassifies two clearly separable verbs

questions.explanation: Anfangen takes the plain verb fangen, which is to catch or capture, and adds the idea of a beginning, so hören auf is the end of a period of listening and school ends at noon. Mitkommen takes kommen and adds the company of a second participant, so mitkommen means to come along with somebody. The prefixes are also visible in the grammar: the first detaches to the end of its clause as auf and the second closes the following clause as mit, which is the same mechanism a learner already knows from aufstehen.
questions.hint: Ask what fangen means on its own, and who mit adds to a plain kommen.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: use age as one cue for choosing a form of address
questions.stem: A visitor asks a woman of about sixty for directions. Which address would a speaker normally try first?

options.text: Sie, because strangers and much older people are addressed formally as a default
du, because a much older person is treated like a friend in any case
options.misconception: believes age alone licenses the informal form with a stranger

options.text: du, because the visitor is younger and may therefore offer it at once
options.misconception: thinks the younger speaker may impose the informal form

options.text: Neither, because a visitor of that age must be addressed with a title
options.misconception: invents a rule about titles where German has none

questions.explanation: Sie is the safe default with anyone a speaker does not know personally, and the gap in years between the two people widens the distance rather than narrowing it, so a much older stranger is addressed formally. The informal du is offered by the person who is older or higher in status, and it is offered, not announced, which is why a learner who offers it unprompted comes across as presumptuous. The real decision is never age alone but whether the two people have agreed, and the agreement is usually arranged with a short question in the first conversation.
questions.hint: Ask which form is safe when nothing has been agreed between the two speakers.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: read the workplace as the setting where the form of address is decided
questions.stem: A new clerk is shown around by a colleague of the same age. What does German practice normally look like in the first weeks?

options.text: Sie between colleagues at first, with du offered by a senior colleague or informally
du straight away, because colleagues of the same age are treated as friends
options.misconception: believes equal age settles the form of address in a workplace

options.text: Sie for a month and du afterwards, with a fixed date set by the office
options.misconception: invents a timetable that no workplace follows

options.text: The last name alone, since German workplaces avoid both pronouns at first
options.misconception: believes German speakers have no way of referring to one another

questions.explanation: A German workplace starts formal. New colleagues, everyone above you and everyone you have not met use Sie, and the informal du is introduced by the person entitled to offer it, often a senior colleague or the team as a whole. In many offices it is done lightly and early, sometimes in a group message, and once it is agreed the du is used with everyone of roughly equal standing rather than only with the person who offered. The useful sentence for a learner to recognise is the offer itself, since it tells them that the decision belongs to the other side.
questions.hint: Ask who is entitled to introduce the informal form in a team.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: treat agreement, not age, as the deciding cue
questions.stem: A student wants to write to a neighbour twice her age and considers 'Darf ich Ihnen du sagen?' What makes that the right move?

options.text: The informal form has to be agreed by both sides, and the question asks for that agreement
The informal form may be used with anyone older once the two have met
options.misconception: believes a single meeting is enough to switch to du

options.text: The informal form is reserved for relatives, so a neighbour could never be offered
options.misconception: restricts du to family and rules out a neighbour entirely

options.text: The question is unnecessary, since Sie is impolite between people of different ages
options.misconception: believes the formal form is an insult whenever ages differ

questions.explanation: The informal form in German is a permission that both sides grant, which is why the offer is a question and not a decision. Darf ich Ihnen du sagen and Wir können uns gerne duzen are the two stock ways of asking, and both leave the answer entirely with the other person, so a negative answer costs nothing socially. Once the du is agreed it is used with that neighbour and the family around them, and the agreement is not withdrawn by a later disagreement, which is why a learner who never asks simply stays on safe formal ground.
questions.hint: Ask who has the right to decide which form of address is used.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: recognise a word that is marked as southern in ordinary use
questions.stem: A shopkeeper in Munich says 'Ich hole zwei Semmeln.' A visitor from Hamburg does not recognise the word. What is going on?

options.text: Die Semmel is a regional word for an ordinary roll, and das Brot is the neutral one
Die Semmel is a northern word for a roll, so the visitor should know it in Hamburg
options.misconception: attaches the word to the wrong region

options.text: Die Semmel is a Swiss term for bread and is not used in Germany
options.misconception: removes the word from the country where it is common

options.text: Die Semmel is a technical term in baking and needs no everyday equivalent
options.misconception: makes a common everyday word sound like jargon

questions.explanation: Die Semmel is the southern and Austrian word for a plain bread roll, and das Brot is the word that works everywhere in Germany. Regional vocabulary is not a matter of error: a speaker from the south is not making a mistake, they are using the word their region uses, and a learner who insists on das Brot alone will be understood but may sound as though they are hiding where they come from. The practical advice is to learn the neutral word first and the marked one afterwards, so both can be recognised without a moment of confusion.
questions.hint: Ask which word a bakery in the far south would put on its list of daily items.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: identify a pair of regional words for the same food
questions.stem: Two shoppers order the same thing. One asks for 'Sahne für den Kaffee' and the other for 'Obers'. What has happened?

options.text: Both mean cream, but die Sahne is the northern and neutral word
Both mean cream, but die Sahne is the southern and das Obers the northern word
options.misconception: reverses the regions attached to the two words

options.text: Sahne means cream and Obers means whipped cream, so the drinks differ
options.misconception: invents a difference in preparation between two names for one thing

options.text: Obers is a brand name and Sahne the generic term for any dairy product
options.misconception: promotes a regional word into a trade mark

questions.explanation: Die Sahne is the word used across most of Germany for cream, while das Obers and, in Austria, der Schlagobers are the southern and Austrian names for the same thing. Both shoppers ordered identical coffee, and the difference tells the listener roughly where the speaker is from. Regional pairs like this one are a normal feature of the language rather than a division into correct and incorrect, and a learner who knows both can follow a conversation in a region without announcing that they are listening from outside it.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two words would appear on a menu printed for a national chain.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: handle a cabbage word that changes with the region
questions.stem: A recipe card from Cologne calls for Rotkohl, and a card from Stuttgart for Rotkraut. Why do the two cookbooks differ?

options.text: Der Kohl and das Kraut are two names for the same dish, marked as northern and southern
Rotkohl and Rotkraut are two dishes, one cooked in the north and one in the south
options.misconception: believes a regional word marks a different recipe rather than a different name

options.text: Das Kraut is the older word and der Kohl a modern trade term in supermarkets
options.misconception: turns a regional pair into a chronological sequence

options.text: Both are incorrect, since the only proper word for red cabbage is der Rotkohl
options.misconception: calls a common regional word an error

questions.explanation: Rotkohl and Rotkraut name one dish, and the choice of noun marks the region of the speaker: der Kohl belongs to the north and central areas while das Kraut is used in the south and in Austria. It is worth noticing that the basic vegetables follow the same pattern, since das Gemüse is neutral, der Kohl and die Bohnen are northern and das Kraut, die Bohne and der Paradeiser are southern. A learner who has the neutral word can cook from either cookbook, and a learner who has the pair can predict which region a speaker is from.
questions.hint: Ask whether a supermarket in Zurich would sell the same name for a red cabbage.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: handle a southern meaning of a word that means something else elsewhere
questions.stem: A speaker from the far south says 'Heute ist mein Bruder nicht gekommen.' A northerner says the sentence means today. What has happened?

options.text: In parts of the south heute means tomorrow, so the brother arrives tomorrow
In parts of the south heute means yesterday, so the brother came earlier
options.misconception: shifts the regional sense a day in the wrong direction

options.text: In parts of the south heute means the whole week, so the sentence is a complaint
options.misconception: inflates a one-day difference into a period

options.text: The sentence is wrong in the south, where the word for tomorrow is also heute
options.misconception: condemns a documented regional usage instead of explaining it

questions.explanation: In a number of southern dialects, including several Alemannic and Bavarian areas, the word that is written heute is used for tomorrow, while the words for today and yesterday take the forms of the two following days. The written language has kept the standard allocation, so a learner reading a printed southern text needs to check which sense the author intends. This case is worth knowing because it is a reminder that a familiar word can carry a different reference in a single region, and that the surrounding words, not the word alone, are what tell a careful reader which sense applies.
questions.hint: Ask what the same dialect would call the day the sentence is spoken on.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.learningObjective: recognise a formula that opens an interruption politely
questions.stem: A visitor wants to ask a question in a seminar. Which opening phrase does German use for that?

options.text: Entschuldigen Sie, which marks the interruption itself and can be used on its own
Ich bin schuld, which asks to be excused for an action already finished
options.misconception: treats a formula for apologising as a way of starting a request

options.text: Sie haben mir geholfen, which thanks somebody for a service just rendered
options.misconception: confuses a thank-you formula with an attention-getter

options.text: Guten Abend, which greets the room and cannot address a single person
options.misconception: believes a greeting cannot be combined with a request

questions.explanation: Entschuldigen Sie is the standard way to interrupt someone politely, and with the formal pronoun it can stand alone, as in Entschuldigen Sie, ich hätte eine Frage. It asks to be excused for interrupting rather than apologising for something already done, which is what a learner who reaches for a word like Entschuldigung tends to get wrong. The informal counterpart is Entschuldigung or, in a familiar register, Entschuldige, and the formula sits at the front of the sentence, with the actual request following it in a normal main clause that has its own verb in second position.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker is sorry about the past or about interrupting now.
